newsitem.title: USA: 30-yr mortgage rates fall to lowest level in over a year.
newsitem.headline: 30-yr mortgage rates fall to lowest level in over a year.

text.p: Average rates on U.S. 30-year home mortgages fell this week to their lowest level in more than 1-1/2 years, Freddie Mac said Thursday.

Thirty-year mortgages in the week fell to an average 7.43 percent, the lowest level since they hit 7.41 percent in the week ended March 1, 1996. Rates for 30-year mortgages stood at 7.47 percent last week.

Fifteen-year fixed-rate mortgages also fell slightly during the week ended July 25, falling to an average 6.98 percent from 7.01 percent last week. The 15-year rate was at its lowest level since the week ended Dec. 6, 1996, when it was at 6.96 percent, Freddie Mac reported.

The fall in mortgage rates can partly be attributed to Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony to House and Senate committees this week, Freddie Mac chief economist Robert Van Order said. Greenspan said growth in the United States appears to be slowing, heading off inflation concerns.

"Chairman Greenspan's remarks earlier in the week greatly reassured the financial markets that inflation is not a threat and the economy is in very good condition," Van Order said in a statement. "Not only did this news help to lower interest rates slightly this week, but it may have the same effect on rates next week."
One-year adjustable rate mortgages were also down slightly, falling to 5.54 percent in the week from 5.55 last week.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 8.19 percent, the 15-year 7.71 percent and the ARM 6.01 percent.

Fees and points charged by lenders for 30-year and 15-year loans slipped to an average 1.7 percent after standing at 1.8 percent last week. ARM loans remained unchanged at 1.4 percent in the July 25 week.
Freddie Mac is a corporation chartered by Congress that buys mortgages from lenders and packages them into securities for investors.
